newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK chemical industry attacks anti-EU stance.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK chemical industry attacks anti-EU stance.

text.p: Leaders of Britain's chemical industry said on Thursday that the increasingly anti-European tone being adopted by the British government was "deeply worrying".

In an interview with Reuters, Elliot Finer, director-general of the Chemical Industries Association (CIA), said the government's negative stance on the European Union (EU) was "terribly harmful" and was damaging the industry's ability to make its voice heard in the rest of Europe.
And Finer said he was worried that the government might take an even more hostile line on Europe as the next general election, which must be called by May 22, approached.

"If as the election campaign develops the Conservatives attempt to differentiate themselves more and more from Labour by taking on a more and more anti-European stance, assuming they mean what they say ...that would be deeply worrying to our members," Finer said.

Although he stressed the association's political impartiality, Finer said the Conservative Party's traditional empathy with industry and business seemed to have been taken over by the opposition Labour Party.

"Every time we speak to Labour politicians we get a huge burst of assurance that they fully understand that it is a global economy and companies pick and choose where they operate. It's only some parts of the Conservative Party that seem not to recognise that," Finer said.
More than a quarter of the British chemical industry's 40 billion pounds annual sales go to Europe, representing over 50 percent of total exports.

Finer expressed alarm at the growing view among some Conservative politicians, including former Chancellor Norman Lamont, that Britain could contemplate withdrawal from the Union. "The ultimate terror would be leaving the EU," Finer said. "It would be extremely damaging to the the UK chemical industry."
The CIA argues that investment in key areas like the car industry, which uses huge amounts of chemicals, would evaporate if Britain pulled out of the EU.
David Culpin, CIA director of business affairs, said that as a result of hostility to the EU Britain was losing its voice in shaping the European economy.

"The U.K.'s voice, which is vital in getting the structures and policies right in Europe, is being sidelined because of the perception of other member states of the semi-detached position of the UK. We are finding difficulty getting our views to be taken as seriously as they should be because the UK is increasingly being seen as semi-detached."

The association is a keen supporter of Britain's early participation in a single currency, which it believes would cut its transaction costs by 200 million pounds a year and eliminate uncertainty over exchange rate movements.
"If we stayed out our biggest worry is that firms that were in the core group would find it more attractive to trade with each other than with companies outside," Finer added.
